fyke.e: Borrowed from Dutch fuik (“fish trap”), from Middle Dutch vuyke, fuke. Cognate with West Frisian fûke, German Low German Fuuk.

ss.fyke net: A type of fish-trap consisting of tubular nets that are supported by hoops.
ss.fyke-net: A type of fish-trap consisting of tubular nets that are supported by hoops.

d.g: A swastika, especially one with the arms bent in an anticlockwise direction.
d.x: Then look at that jade fylfot charm pawned for one-and-three down at the Basin and the use that could have been made of it in the Kharkov 'ritual murder' trial.

fylfot.e: Uncertain, but likely from Middle English fillen (“to fill”) (from Old English fyllan) + fot (“foot”) (from Old English fōt), in reference to its use as a design to be placed at the bottom of stained-glass windows.

d.g: Vegetation unique to the Cape Floral Kingdom, largely scrub, exceptionally biodiverse, including particularly large numbers of species of Proteaceae, Restionaceae, and Ericaceae.
d.x: The southern and western Cape is the home of a unique type of vegetation known as fynbos. Covering around 90 000 square kilometers of often harsh terrain, fynbos is made up of approximately 6 000 different plant species.

fynbos.e: From Afrikaans fynbos (“fynbos”), from fyn (“fine”) (as in fine-textured, as opposed to trees) and bos (“bush or forest”).

d.g: The monetary unit of Sweden between the 15th and 17th centuries, valued at between one-sixth and one-half of an öre.

fyrk.e: From Swedish fyrk, from Middle Low German vêreken, from ver/vier (“four”).

d.g: Any biological organism having extended functions provided by technology
An English militiaman of the Saxon period; often a land worker called to arms in support of the king or a local lord, and usually armed with a spear and shield.

fyrdman.e: Learned borrowing from Old English fyrdmann, fierdmann (“warrior”), from fierd (“army”) + mann (“man”). More at fyrd, man.
